newsitem.title: HUNGARY: NEW YEAR MORTAR ATTACK WORRIES BUDAPEST POLICE.
newsitem.headline: NEW YEAR MORTAR ATTACK WORRIES BUDAPEST POLICE.

text.p: Hungarian police on Thursday said they were worried by the use of an anti-tank mortar which failed to go off at a New Year party in the latest in a spate of explosions in Budapest.
"This is the first time in the history of the Hungarian police we've had to deal with such a weapon," Budapest police spokesman Endre Nagy told Reuters.

A Yugoslav-made shoulder-launched armour-piercing grenade failed to go off in the early hours of Wednesday morning when it was fired into an empty flat above a night club where owners and employees were celebrating New Year.
No-one was hurt and damage amounted to only $2,000, police said.
Nagy said if the World-War-Two-era mortar had exploded there would have been many casualties.
"This is an anti-tank weapon - with this it is possible to demolish a whole building," he said. "If it had hit the ground floor and gone off, at least 15 people would have been killed."

He added that judging from where the mortar appeared to have been fired, the attacker may have deliberately targeted the first floor of the building rather than the club itself in order to frighten the owners rather than kill them.
"From where we found remnants of the launcher only the upper part of the building was in his sights," he said. "He may have deliberately missed the night club."

Nagy said that police were not ruling out a link with a series of grenade attacks over the last three months which have damaged property -- mainly night clubs and massage parlours -- but have not caused any injuries.
Two businessmen thought to be linked to organised crime have also been murdered.

Following the police's failure to solve the crimes, the Hungarian government sacked the chiefs of the national and Budapest police forces in November, then appointed officers from outside Budapest to replace them.
Interior Minister Gabor Kuncze was quoted as saying there were no suitable candidates for either post among the capital's 8,000-strong force.

New national police chief Laszlo Forgacs, 47, who previously headed the force of Hungary's poorest county Borsod-Abauj-Zemplen, promised new initiatives on his appointment last month but asked for patience as results would not come quickly.
